clinicalPearls: A membrane bridging the vocal folds anteriorly, most commonly at the anterior commissure, that may be congenital or acquired
Congenital webs present in infancy with a weak or abnormal cry, stridor, and variable airway obstruction
Acquired webs typically follow bilateral mucosal injury at the anterior commissure, such as after simultaneous surgery on both folds, trauma, or intubation
Symptoms depend on web thickness and extent, ranging from mild hoarseness to significant airway compromise
Congenital anterior webs are associated with 22q11.2 deletion, so consider assessment for associated anomalies
Diagnosis is by laryngoscopy, with the subglottic extent and thickness of the web guiding management
Management ranges from endoscopic division of thin webs to more complex reconstruction with keel placement or laryngofissure for thick webs
reference.pathophysiology: A glottic web is a band of tissue joining the anterior portions of the vocal folds. Congenital webs arise from incomplete recanalisation of the primitive laryngeal lumen during embryonic development, when the transiently fused epithelial lamina fails to fully separate. Acquired webs form when opposing raw mucosal surfaces at the anterior commissure heal together, as occurs after bilateral vocal fold surgery, caustic or thermal injury, or repeated intubation trauma, so a fibrous adhesion bridges the folds. The web restricts independent vibration and, if bulky, narrows the glottic aperture, producing dysphonia and, in thicker or more extensive lesions, airway obstruction.
additionalDifferentials: Recurrent respiratory papillomatosis bridging the commissure
Anterior commissure scarring from prior surgery
additionalInvestigations: Flexible fibreoptic laryngoscopy to identify and characterise the web
Rigid endoscopy under anaesthesia to assess thickness and subglottic extension
Videostroboscopy to evaluate the effect on vocal fold vibration
Genetic evaluation for 22q11.2 deletion in congenital anterior webs
Imaging or bronchoscopy to define associated airway anomalies where suspected
redFlags: Stridor or respiratory distress from a thick or extensive web
A neonate with an abnormal or absent cry and airway compromise
Subglottic extension indicating a more complex reconstructive problem
Recurrent webbing after repair, suggesting inadequate mucosal resurfacing
reference.prognosis: Thin anterior webs divided endoscopically generally do well with good voice and airway outcomes, whereas thick webs with subglottic extension are prone to recurrence and often need staged reconstruction with more guarded voice results.
pitfalls: Simply dividing a web without measures to prevent re-adhesion of the raw surfaces
Underestimating subglottic extension and thickness, leading to inadequate surgery
Missing an associated 22q11.2 deletion in a congenital case
Performing simultaneous bilateral anterior commissure surgery, which itself creates acquired webs
references: Cummings Otolaryngology: Head and Neck Surgery
Scott-Brown's Otorhinolaryngology, Head and Neck Surgery
management: Endoscopic division of thin anterior webs, often with placement of a keel or mucosal flap to prevent the raw edges re-fusing
Staged open laryngotracheal reconstruction for thick webs with subglottic extension
Secure the airway in significant obstruction, with tracheostomy for severe congenital webs presenting with stridor in infancy
Voice and speech therapy after intervention to optimise the vocal outcome
Genetic evaluation for 22q11.2 deletion in congenital anterior webs, with assessment for associated anomalies
Surveillance laryngoscopy for restenosis or re-formation, which is common with thicker lesions
Manage through a laryngology and paediatric ENT multidisciplinary team
